articles.headline: Are Screens Making Us Dumber? The Science Schools Won't Talk About
articles.body: Teachers say students no longer push through hard problems on their own. They just Google it. The National Assessment of Educational Progress has shown a rapid decline in students’ reading and math scores within the last six years, with some of the lowest results ever recorded. Reading scores in 2024 fell 5 points, or roughly half a grade level, from 2019 levels for both fourth and eighth graders. Math dropped 3 points for fourth graders and 8 points, or roughly a full grade level, for eighth graders over the same period. For state level comparison, between 2019 and 2024, no states improved eighth grade reading scores. Thirty-eight states saw declines. For eighth grade math, 49 out of 50 states saw scores drop. According to Common Sense Media, teens currently spend an average of eight and a half hours a day on screens outside of school — an average that has risen significantly in the past six years. However, according to CNN, adolescent teens are spending 70 minutes every school day on their phones, and that’s not counting laptops. Neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath has spent years studying how the brain processes and stores information. His conclusion on classroom technology is not what most school districts want to hear. “Even in schools, it doesn’t matter what the size of the screen is,” Horvath testified in a hearing titled “Plugged Out: Examining the Impact of Technology on America's Youth,” on Jan. 15. “All of these things are going to hurt learning, which in turn are going to hurt our kids’ cognitive development.” According to Horvath, by 2024, the United States had spent more than $30 billion on putting screens in classrooms, with school districts making deals to buy laptops and tablets at a discounted rate. The push began in the early 2000s, when Maine became the first state to launch a statewide laptop program: the Maine Learning Technology Initiative. Schools have not slowed down their spending on technology as many billions of dollars continue to go toward tablets, smartboards and laptops every year, with the idea that newer technology leads to better learning. A study discovered that students engaged in off-task activities on their computers nearly two-thirds of the time. Horvath pointed to this as a key reason technology slows learning, saying that when attention is interrupted, it takes time to refocus, and task-switching is linked to weaker memory formation. Patricia Jacobsen, mathematics department chair at Sacramento Country Day, has watched the shift happen in real time. “I think it’s more difficult for some students to really lock in with their laptops in front of them,” Jacobsen said. Beyond just staying focused, Jacobsen said she has noticed students struggling to push through difficult material on their own without technology. Jacobsen is torn on the issue of technology. Some students, she said, have parents, siblings or the money to hire a tutor when they are struggling. “What if you're the kid who doesn't have any of that?” That is where she sees technology earning its place. Tools like Khan Academy, she said, open doors for students who would otherwise have nowhere to turn. Jacobsen described a student who had always been permitted to use a four-function calculator and, as a result, never learned how to work with negative numbers. When the student encountered a problem requiring basic integer arithmetic, they could not solve it. “They’ve never been encouraged or taught how to deal with negative five minus eight,” Jacobsen said. “Students are less likely to focus in class, ask questions or come visit me during flex because everybody knows if they ever have a question, they can just Google it or use PhotoMath or AI to get close enough to the answer,” Jacobsen said. Jacobsen said technology should work the same way any other convenience does. It makes certain tasks easier, but it should never replace the underlying skill. In her own classroom, she requires students to learn how to solve problems by hand before they are permitted to use a calculator. “You need to learn how to do it, then you use the tool,” she said. “But nowadays it’s like, ‘Why would I learn how to do that? I can just do it on my calculator. Why do I learn how to factor? The calculator factors for me.’” As of 2024, about a third of eighth graders nationwide are failing to reach the basic benchmark in reading — the largest percentage ever recorded on the test, according to the National Assessment of Educational Progress. Education officials have poured money into tutoring programs and intervention efforts since the pandemic with public schools spending more than $27 billion on tutoring and summer learning and $30 billion on staffing these intervention programs, according to the U.S. Department of Education's The Pandemic Learning Project. Twelfth grade reading scores peaked in 2009 and fell significantly in the following decade. The trend, researchers say, points to something deeper than COVID-19 learning loss. Twelfth grade math peaked in 2013 and also declined by 2019, well before the pandemic disrupted schools. Whether school districts will reconsider how they approach classroom technology remains unclear. American schools spend anywhere between $26 billion to $41 billion on education technology every year and that number will continue to climb, according to the nonprofit EdTech Evidence Exchange. Some universities are already pushing back. Faced with widespread AI cheating, professors have begun returning to handwritten exams. Bluebook sales at the University of Florida rose 50% in the 2024-2025 school year, jumping to 80% at UC Berkeley, according to the Wall Street Journal. “The point of getting an education is not to have the most efficient, easy process along the way,” Jonathan Senchyne, a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, said. “The point is to challenge yourself.”

articles.headline: Coyote Creek solar project faces environmental opposition
articles.body:
Coyote Creek News

By RYAN XU and KHIVI SINGH

According to Kate Kelly — a consultant for Defenders of Wildlife and an expert on renewable energy policy planning and siting issues — the Coyote Creek project “all went wrong when SMUD entered into a power purchase agreement with this project in advance of any environmental review or consideration.” The Coyote Creek Agrovoltaic Ranch, more commonly referred to as Coyote Creek, is a planned solar farm — located along Scott Road north of Rancho Murieta — that has generated controversy. The Solar Energy Industries Association defines a solar power purchase agreement as “a financial agreement where a developer arranges for the design, permitting, financing and installation of a solar energy system on a customer’s property,” and the developer sells the power generated back to the customer at a fixed rate. For the Coyote Creek Project, the customer is the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD) and the developer is D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI). According to the 2021 power purchasing agreement between SMUD and DESRI, the completion of permitting and the start of construction on the project was scheduled for June 2022. The project sparked conflict with environmentalists over its impact on the habitat. Hy Martin — DESRI chief development officer — said the property was chosen for the project because “it was considered low-value grazing land,” the Sacramento Bee reported in December 2024. Advanced Topics in Environmental Studies teacher Caroline Hersh-Rodeen, who attended the November city council meeting, said that she was confused by the planned location. “Out of all places, why here? That’s what was never truly answered through any of the city council meetings.” Kelly, who has spent 15 years reviewing solar projects across California, shares that skepticism. “The impacts of this project are exceptional,” Kelly said. “This is one of the three or four very worst that we’ve ever seen in that time.” The project would construct 500,000 solar panels over 2,700 acres — enough to power about 45,000 households under SMUD’s jurisdiction. In order to flatten the site for development, 1.3 million cubic yards of land would need to be excavated. This process would cause substantial disruption to vernal pool habitats, cultural and archeological resources, and the removal of old-growth blue oak trees. The project will result in the loss of 3,493 oak trees, with the largest having an estimated age of 850 years with a chest-height diameter of 67 inches, according to Kelly and a press release by the California Native Plant Society (CNPS). “This level of environmental destruction to accommodate this project is beyond acceptable,” Kelly said. In November 2025, the Sacramento County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the project, following a 6-hour hearing where a majority of 130 speakers opposed the proposal. “I was really disheartened when I walked away from the County Board of Supervisors meeting, and I felt like that they heard comment after comment after comment of people with concerns about the environment and when it was their opportunity to respond, not one of them touched on it,” Gabrielle Katanic, an influencer aiding the Save Coyote Creek coalition who was present at the board meeting, said. Following the approval of the project, Coyote Creek has come under a wave of legal challenges, focused around the project’s Environmental Impact Report (EIR). Under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an EIR must be prepared for any project which may cause substantial environmental change. “The EIR of the project is deeply flawed, and there are now three lawsuits on the adequacy of that EIR,” Kelly said. CNPS, alongside the Environmental Council of Sacramento, filed a lawsuit against the County of Sacramento on Dec. 18, 2025. The suit cites “numerous deficiencies in the project’s Final Environmental Impact Report,” and that the report “is so deeply flawed that it is insufficient to support informed decision-making.” Wilton Rancheria, the only federally recognized Native American tribe in the Sacramento area, filed a suit against the County of Sacramento alleging violations of the CEQA the next day. The tribe represents both the Miwok and Nisenan people. The suit alleges that the project violates cultural and environmental protections. At the same time, the California Four Wheel Drive Association also filed a suit against the county, for the same reasons as CNPS, allegeding that the county “unlawfully certified a legally deficient Final Environmental Impact Report” according to a press release on the group’s website. The project is currently unable to proceed due to the ongoing litigation regarding the EIR. As such, the permitting process has stalled. “The project’s in a bit of a limbo right now. It can’t really pull permits, same on the federal side, where we have policies coming out of this administration that have basically blocked processing of solar and wind projects,” Kelly said. On Jan. 5, SMUD canceled its power purchasing agreement with DESRI. The decision was made due to “supply chain constraints, rising prices, tariffs, schedule delays, environmental impacts and pending litigation” according to a press release on SMUD’s website (www.smud.org). DESRI will continue with the project, though due to the ongoing litigation and lack of permits, construction will be unable to proceed until lawsuits end, which may take years. “Developers generally rely on a fairly complex series of financing maneuvers and loans. They’re not going to be able to get financing on this project, or it’s going to be very difficult for them to finance any activity when there’s uncertainty on a lawsuit,” Kelly said. Kelly points to other locations that could be alternatively developed, including places with exhausted farmland or where other developments can’t occur. “We have places in South Sacramento Country where there were a lot of wine grapes, and a lot of those grapes are getting removed. There’s also parking lots, warehouses and landfills.” Kelly also points to another proposal which would place solar panels above aqueducts and canals, which would decrease evaporation and improve the efficiency of the panels. Hersh said that the location picked and the subsequent environmental damage would not make sense. “Why would we pick one of the few remaining pristine habitats in Sacramento county as a location to make clean energy which is theoretically for the benefit of that environment?”

articles.headline: Online Sports Gambling Must Be Regulated
articles.body:
Online Sports Gambling Must Be Regulated D2

Ryan Hobbs, Sacramento Country Day middle school dean of students, is worried about his students’ attitudes toward sports betting. While he hasn’t witnessed any students placing sports bets, he has seen many instances of kids as young as 11 joking about doing so. “One of the kids in my elective pulled up all of the prop bets for the Super Bowl, and students were taking turns saying what they would have bet for each of the prop bets,” he said. U.S. adults have a substantial gambling problem. According to the National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG), 2.5 million Americans in 2024 were addicted to sports gambling, and the number continues to rise. Online searches for gambling addiction help increased by about 23% in the U.S. following the expansion of legalized sports betting in 2018, according to a University of California San Diego study from 2016-2024. One-fifth of the adult male population is or have been in debt from sports betting, according to the Center for Public Justice. The American Institute for Boys and Men noted an average increase of $30 of debt per consumer due to sports gambling. The NCPG warns that those addicted to sports betting are 26 times more likely to commit suicide than people who haven’t placed a sports bet. Hobbs says he is concerned about the negative effects Cavaliers joking about the issue today could have on their futures. “You can’t just let kids loose on this stuff, right? Gambling ruins people’s lives. In an alternate future where it is a problem, schools should handle it the same way as a kid doing drugs.” A New Age of Sports Gambling Sports gambling has existed for millennia, from people wagering on chariot races in the 6th century B.C.E. to sports leagues in the 21st century. While it had been banned in the U.S. for years, in May 2018, the Supreme Court overturned the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act (PASPA), officially legalizing online sports gambling for people over 21. Now, professional sports leagues such as the NFL and NBA began partnering with betting platforms such as FanDuel and DraftKings. Sports that prohibit their own players, coaches and staff from sports betting increasingly push betting commercials and content across social media and television. Sophomore Lucas Holz, a sports fan, has seen many sports betting ads and is concerned about how betting companies sell their products. “On TikTok, the videos I see promote sports-betting talk about how much you can win, never about the potential losses that come with betting,” he said. He also mentioned that every “three scrolls,” a betting ad seems to pop up. “That could really influence teens to make bad decisions with their money and lose it all in one place.”

Increase in Underage Sports Gambling

The issue of underage sports gambling is prevalent even in California, a state that has made most forms of sports gambling illegal for youth and adults. An increasing number of teens use apps like PrizePicks or crypto-based sites to bet on player props (proposition bets), which are wagers on specific individual player statistics or milestones within a game, rather than bets on the final outcome. Despite California Attorney General Rob Bonta classifying player props as “unlawful sports wagering” in a 2025 legal opinion, companies that offer these bets still operate in the state. The Casino Control Commission told USA Today that since 2023, DraftKings “by far” had the most reports of underage activity (620), collecting $2.78 million in wagers by suspected underage users since 2023. In the same span, FanDuel had 162 underage reports, “accounting for $63,152 in bets.” The same investigation found that around 70% of teenagers have placed an online bet, with a growing number becoming addicted to gambling. The USA Today investigative reporter who authored the piece, Nick Penzenstadler, reported how easy it is for minors to start betting on sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. “When you make an account, you need to have a real person with a real social security number, a bank account and an address. And they check all that to make sure you’re of age, usually 18 or 21,” he writes. There are ways around the safeguards, Penzenstadler reports — for example by borrowing someone’s identity (or stealing it) or uploading a parent’s identification or an older sibling’s ID card. A 2024 survey conducted at Redwood High School in Larkspur, Calif., determined that nearly three-fourths of male students and one-fourth of female students had placed a sports bet on an online platform despite being underage. Redwood students admitted anonymously to using Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) to claim they were located in other parts of the country and even North America as a whole. VPNs allow users to get around regulations in one’s own state and access sites that are allowed in other parts of the continent. Forty-three Country Day high school students filled out a similar poll for The Octagon on March 24, with about half — 51% — of respondents reporting placing a sports bet. Additionally, 42% have seen over 11 sports-betting ads per day, and 88% have come across at least one per day.

Legislation and Action Sites like Kalshi and Polymarket, which are considered “prediction markets,” or global betting markets on future events, are still permitted to operate in California. Both platforms cater to a teenage audience through paying popular content creators to talk about their platform, as well as through TikTok-style, high volume ads. Polymarket in particular is under intense scrutiny after they offered betting on when U.S. soldiers who were shot down in Iran would be rescued, according to NBC News. While they took this specific bet down, Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton added that the platform has 219 other war bets active. A similar site, Kalshi, refused to pay out $54 million in bets regarding the removal of Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. This triggered a lawsuit and heavy backlash towards the company. California legislators Pilar Schiavo and Mia Bonta plan to introduce Assembly Bill 2617 — Protecting Kids From Online Gambling Act. This bill would ban platforms like FanDuel and DraftKings from both marketing to minors and allowing them to play. The proposal highlights that youth “are more susceptible to reward-driven decisionmaking, impulsivity and risk-taking behaviors, increasing vulnerability to future problem gambling and associated financial and mental health harms.” If it were to pass the legislature, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. The bill makes sure only approved operators — tribal casinos, licensed entities or state-authorized platforms — could legally offer sports betting. Platforms would need to follow strict rules on age verification (21+) and tracking to ensure bets happen inside California. Unlicensed apps or offshore sportsbooks would be illegal. However, nearly 81% of young people have already been exposed to sports gambling advertisements according to the Journal of Behavioral Addictions, and despite, according to the Journal of Behavioral Addictions, four out of five teens believing the advertisements should be restricted, little change has occurred. The California Office of Problem Gambling identified several tells for budding gambling addictions. “You might notice you are playing longer than you meant to, checking your phone constantly, or feeling pulled back in even when you want to stop. You might feel stressed, irritated, or restless when you are not playing. You might spend money to try to get a better outcome or a bigger haul,” their website reported. The NCPG provides resources for those struggling with gambling problems, including “answers to commonly asked questions, a gambling behavior self assessment, information about treatment and the National Problem Gambling Helpline (1-800-MY-RESET).” The NCPG website encourages problem gamblers or those who know them to seek help.

articles.headline: Soccer van crash injures Country Day student
articles.body:
Soccer van crash injures CD student

By Jacob Rabe and Khivi Singh Editor-in-Chief and Section Editor

On April 16, a semi-truck struck one of two Suburbans carrying the Sacramento Country Day girls soccer team, hospitalizing freshman Maya Rajuan. The two Ford Suburbans, driven by head coach George Champayne and assistant coach Jason Allen, left around 2:30 p.m. and were headed to Faith Christian School (FCS) in Yuba City. Their match against FCS was scheduled for 4 p.m. and would determine whether they made the playoffs. Rajuan, along with freshmen Lyla Sandlin and Casey Mahoney and sophomore Rorey Mahoney, rode with Champayne. Between 2018 and 2023, the California Statewide Integrated Traffic Records System recorded 154 fatal and serious injury crashes on I-5 and 165 on the adjoining Highway 99 in Sacramento County. The California Highway Patrol classifies serious injury as including broken bones, severe lacerations, internal injuries and unconsciousness at the scene, among other criteria. Traveling north on I-5 towards Arena Blvd and Del Paso Blvd, Champayne was following Allen’s Suburban at about 35 miles an hour — the freeway was backed up, he said. As they prepared to merge onto Highway 99, both vehicles pulled into the right lane. Allen stopped. Champayne stopped, leaving a one to two car gap between them. “Within a second after I stopped,” Champayne said, “the semi came behind and clipped us from the corner [of the Suburban].” In the van ahead, Allen heard the impact and watched Champayne’s Suburban shift. Champayne called out, “Are we okay?” Rajuan was unresponsive. “Her head busted the glass out of the Suburban, popped the glass right out. It was a loud crunch sound,” Champayne said. “Some cops came, assessed the situation, took my information, and then they said that I needed an ambulance,” Rajuan said. “They took me to the hospital for the night, where I got tests. I had nerve and muscle damage, a concussion, trauma to the body, bruises and cuts.” Following the collision, Champayne and Athletic Director Matt Vargo chose to postpone the soccer match. Vargo brought another van to transport students back to school. “I don’t think we’ve had an accident like this for over 10 years,” Head of School Lee Thomsen said. “I’ve been here for 10 years and I don’t recall anything like this happening.” Chief Financial Officer Bill Petchauer and Director of Transportation Jay Holman were handling the incident while Thomsen was out of town. Thomsen acknowledged the school fell short in one area. “We could have done a better job of following up with families and kids later that day or in the evening, just to, you know — if the accident occurred at 2 o’clock, to call at 7 and be like, ‘hey, just checking in,’” Thomsen said. “As I understand the police report so far,” Thomsen said, “our van was traveling as it should and was rear-ended by the truck.” Rajuan sat out the remainder of the soccer season and received academic accommodations, including for her finals. “I just get one question at a time,” Rajuan said. “Once my brain gets blurry, I’ll take a break and come back.” The crash raised questions about Country Day’s concussion protocols. Under California Education Code (EDC) § 49475, private schools offering athletic programs must require athletes to sign a concussion and head injury information sheet annually and complete a graduated return-to-play protocol — staged physical activity before an athlete resumes full contact — of no less than seven days following a concussion. Country Day’s handbook satisfies neither requirement; it only asks student-athletes to “submit a form to Country Day indicating a physical evaluation has been completed,” mentioning neither a concussion information sheet nor a graduated return-to-play protocol. Nearby private schools Jesuit High School and Christian Brothers High School both maintain explicit concussion protocols. Reached for comment, Thomsen responded via email. "Country Day takes concussions very seriously, and we do follow concussion protocols. All of our coaches are required to take a concussion in sports certification through the National Federation of State High School Associations. In every case where one occurs with a Country Day athlete, which is rare, we work with their medical professionals to ensure a safe return to the classroom or field.” On Rajuan’s specific accommodations, he wrote: “For all students with concussions, we ask for and follow the recommendations of their medical professional. In this case, the student did not return to athletics, has limited screen use, and has extended time/exemptions on academic work, as per the medical documentation.” He acknowledged one gap. “In the past, we distributed an athletic concussion paper information sheet to all families of athletes. It appears we have not included that in our handbook, and we will do so as we make our annual revisions this summer,” Thomsen wrote. Because Rajuan’s concussion occurred during transit rather than an athletic activity, the statute’s return-to-play requirements would not have applied to her situation specifically. Champayne has served as the head coach of girls soccer at Country Day since 1995. The crash settled a decision he’d been considering. “When I went to Sacramento Country Day, it kind of felt like family. So when we got hit, the thoughts that came to my mind were, ‘I don’t want to put myself in that position again,’” Champayne said. “That kind of made me make my decision to retire.” He had already been planning to retire alongside his wife and travel — after 31 years, he said, it was just time. “I just didn’t want to put myself in a position with having seven, eight girls in the car and something happening,” Champayne said. On April 20, the girls soccer team won 5-2 in their rescheduled game against FCS.

articles.headline: AI data centers raise energy and climate questions
articles.body:
AI Data Center Story D1

Half of Sacramento Country Day high school students use artificial intelligence (AI) weekly, according to an April 28 poll sent out by The Octagon. Students use AI to help search for information, check grammar and summarize documents, reported the Digital Education Council. The environmental impacts of AI, however — specifically the data centers that run them — include using large amounts of water, burning fossil fuels and decreasing local air quality. “Why can’t we create a system such that we use this beautiful new tool that took so many scientists so long to develop in a way that doesn’t directly harm the planet?” Sacramento Country Day’s computer science and environmental science teacher, Caroline Hersh-Rodeen, said.

Environment IBM defines an AI data center as “a facility that houses the specific IT infrastructure needed to train, deploy and deliver AI applications and services.” Before they can be put into use, AI models need to be trained to recognize patterns in large data sets, a process that requires running computations and adjusting billions of parameters in these data centers. Some models take multiple months to train, continuously running thousands of computer chips at the same time. This process requires a lot of energy. According to research published in MIT Technology Review — an online magazine published by Massachusetts Institute of Technology — GPT-4’s training is estimated to have taken enough energy to power San Francisco for three days. After the AI is trained, users can input questions that the AI answers by sorting through the patterns in the data and outputting the results calculated. These complex processes require advanced computer chips. According to the Pew Research Center (PRC), some of them take two to four times more watts to run compared to a standard chip and require large amounts of water for cooling. Rough estimates from organizations like that of University of California, Riverside claim that water usage from California data centers alone reached 49.9 billion tons as of 2023, with that number set to increase. The creator of the organization Internet Of Water, a movement and data infrastructure designed to make public water data open, discoverable and digitally accessible, Peter Colohan, shared in an interview that wherever companies choose to put a data center, it is like a “giant soda straw sucking water out of local basins around the world.” The impact of data centers is not limited to water. The Kapor Foundation, a nonprofit organization focused on making technology more accessible, estimates that by 2030, 1,300 premature deaths, accounting for over 33% of asthma-related deaths, across the United States will be because of data centers’ diesel-powered generators, which produce a toxic chemical called diesel particulate matter (PM). The foundation cites that 82% of data centers are located in communities with poor air quality in California — measured by diesel PM levels — as well as areas with “groundwater threats, and high concentrations of hazardous waste, potentially exacerbating harm to these communities.” Kapor Foundation also highlights Del Paso Heights in Sacramento, a neighborhood that has reported high amounts of poverty and pollution. It has led to some of the highest asthma rates in California, with one neighborhood in the 100th percentile. Within a few miles of Del Paso Heights, there are two data center campuses: one totaling 52.7 megawatts (MW) and another totaling 26 MW. NTT Data Center Campus was built in 2015 and Prime Data Center Campus was completed in 2020, both of which have likely led to heightened respiratory illnesses in the area, per the Kapor Foundation.

AI usage and energy requirements become concerns

Junior Matthew Inman said that his classmates’ frequent use of AI frightens him. “When I was preparing for a Bio[logy] test earlier this year, I asked a classmate who did particularly well, ‘how did you do so well?’” Inman said. Their answer: AI. With over 200 million more weekly users using ChatGPT in February 2026 compared to September 2025 according to OpenAI’s website, advancements in the AI tech sector are necessary — especially in California. Silicon Valley has become a hub for data centers — Santa Clara alone possesses 57 active or under-construction data centers. With the uptick in AI users, these centers now require more power than before. According to the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, a nonprofit think tank focused on land use, Meta’s Hyperion data center in Louisiana is set to require twice the power of the city of New Orleans once completed. Hersh-Rodeen doesn’t put the blame on the consumers, but rather the environmental policies in place. “When we have societal problems, there is an inclination to blame the individual and their use of a certain product, rather than blame and then take action to change the system that created this problem, and I think that that is a dangerous mistake to make as a society,” Hersh-Rodeen said. “The people who benefit from this system continue to benefit from it because it’s not changed.” In 2025, California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a proposal that would have required data center operators to report their water use, even after the bill was weakened. Newsom signed one data-center-related measure that year, which allowed regulators to determine whether data centers are driving up costs. “Getting rid of AI is only going to lower us back to what was already unsustainable,” Hersh-Rodeen said. “We really need to work on lowering [environmental impacts] overall, and I think that that's a piece that is missing out of a lot of the outrage.”

Looking Forward Because of the amount of energy needed to support AI data centers, many companies create their own power sources — either from fossil fuel plants or more environmentally-friendly options, like wind farms or solar. AI data centers also have the option to pull from local grids, which are often powered by fossil fuels. Dave Tamayo is the president of the board of directors at the Sacramento Municipal Security District (SMUD) — a community-owned, not-for-profit electric utility provider for Sacramento County and small parts of Placer and Yolo counties in California. “We can’t actually control where they get their energy from, but what we are doing is we’re working with folks to make sure that they understand what their options are,” Tamayo said. “If they come into Sacramento, and they want to build their own generation behind the meter, that means that they own it, and we can’t tell them what to do, but we can set requirements on how they interact with our system.” Some power companies have begun to shift their energy sources to renewable energy, with SMUD having a goal of 100% carbon free energy by 2030. AI data centers can strain local grids by drawing mass amounts of power, but the data centers can also support them with the right infrastructure. “AI isn’t just a really large load, a big draw on our system,” Tamayo said. “If they put in the right type of electrical generation or batteries on their site, that can be very valuable to helping us run the grid more efficiently. If they have more energy than they need, then they can sell it to us and use it to support our grid when we need that energy.” Hersh-Rodeen said that AI data centers using renewable energy would make her feel better about using AI. “If we had different power sources, it wouldn’t be using fossil fuels and thus contributing to climate change. It would be using the wind or the sun or something. And then I wouldn’t feel bad about using it because sunlight is everywhere. It’s not causing a problem,” she said. Tamayo hopes that engineering events that SMUD hosts — such as Solar Regatta, a solar-powered boat competition — will encourage the next generation of innovators to invent more sustainable technologies. “I’m really looking forward to learning about how the young people here [at Solar Regatta] go on,” Tamayo said. “We really need people to be interested in this, and it’s an exciting field. Rebuilding the energy system for the entire country is an exciting prospect.”

articles.headline: Octagon staffers earn six national journalism awards
articles.body: On April 16-19, 15 Octagon staffers and three Medallion staffers attended the 2026 National High School Journalism Convention (NHSJC) in Minneapolis. This year, seven Sacramento Country Day students competed on-site in the Journalism Education Association’s National Student Media Contests (NSMC); six took home an award. The NHSJC hosted 5,000 student journalists from a variety of schools nationwide. At NHSJC, students spent the two days of the trip attending various writing workshops, speaker events and media critiques. On April 17, seven students from Country Day participated in the onsite NSMC. Each competitor got two hours to complete their article, provided with paper, a pencil, a dictionary, an AP style guide and a recording device if an interview was needed. Notable entries were ranked either “Honorable Mention,” “Excellent” or “Superior.” Octagon staffers earned a Superior award, two Excellent awards and three Honorable Mentions. This year Octagon reporters sophomore Parsiny Nijher and juniors Lukas Chung and Noor Alameri won Honorable Mention in their various competitions: Alameri for Review Writing, Chung for Feature Writing and Nijher for Sports Writing. Judges presented two Excellent awards to Octagon staffers: junior Kate Barnes for Editorial Writing and sophomore Maddy Schank for News Editing/Current Events/Headline Writing. Sophomore Sid Shukla competed in the Commentary Writing contest. Because he had no experience in on-site competition, Shukla was nervous going into the competition. “With the cold prompt, I didn’t know what to expect. I felt pretty unprepared and nervous but also excited since it was my first ever time competing,” he said. Despite his apprehension, Shukla earned Country Day’s only Superior award. “My initial reaction was shock, since after they announced the excellent and honorable mention people I genuinely didn’t have any hope,” Shukla said. When asked what advice he would give to the future competitors, he said that students shouldn’t rely on technology when writing pieces. “You don’t get a computer in the competition, so you can’t check for any grammar mistakes or anything like that and you need to know AP style,” he said. Octagon adviser Andrea Todd explains that she specifically lobbied Shukla to participate in the Commentary Writing competition based on his experience. “The only person I asked to do the contest was Sid. I asked Sid to do the commentary writing because he expresses his opinions very eloquently,” she said. “He texted me ahead of time about the contest and what it would be like, what he should do and how he could prepare.” Upon hearing about the six awards, Todd was “amazed.” “I had to get up and leave before the winners were announced for each of our categories because of our dinner reservations, but I’m just so proud. I couldn’t believe it when I heard six out of seven won an award,” she said. This year was freshman Khivi Singh’s first year participating in NHSJC. Singh will be The Octagon’s feature section editor for the 2026-27 school year. Singh said the experience was an educational one. “I had really high hopes, and I knew that I was going to learn a lot, and I did. So I picked a lot of classes that I felt aligned with my new position on The Octagon and with my general interests,” she said. NHSJC hosted yearbook staffers as well and proved beneficial for Medallion staffers, according to junior Aziza Halim. Halim, current assistant editor-in-chief of Country Day’s yearbook, the Medallion, attended the NHSJC for the second time. Halim decided to attend again because of the educational advantages one can gain from the classes at the convention center. “I know this journalism trip offered classes for both writing and yearbook. So I looked at the classes they offered, like photography, and did yearbook-focused classes,” she said. Halim described this experience as a great opportunity to meet yearbook staff from different schools in different states. “I got to connect with other editors in the yearbook, which is the same position I have. I just met a bunch of people, and it was really nice to see different perspectives,” she said. Students also got an opportunity to explore Minneapolis by venturing to the Mississippi River or taking the metro rail to the Mall of America. One memorable restaurant experience was at “The Newsroom,” which the whole group dined at on the last night of the trip. “Overall, my favorite part of the trip was being able to finish classes super early and just explore the city, go to different places, and watch five movies per night with my friends,” Shukla said. Todd concluded that the spring 2026 NHSJC was a success for The Octagon as a whole. “I think [the convention] bodes well for the future of the paper, and I think next year is going to be even better,” Todd said.

articles.headline: New Student Leadership Positions declared for the year of 2026-27
articles.body: New positions have been announced for Student Council, The Octagon and The Medallion for the 2026-27 school year. The high school Student Council, which oversees school events and activities, has selected the students who will take over from the current student body leaders. President senior Gavin Wang and vice president senior Liam Donohue selected juniors Justin Lawson and Diana Haus to become co-presidents. “Justin is a charismatic leader, and he’s on top of everything. Because he is approachable, he’s able to get more people involved in school events such as rallies and games,” Donohue said. “Diana, on the other hand, is an experienced member of Student Council. She’s very good at managing the finer details of activities.” Patricia Jacobsen, Student Council adviser and high school dean of student life, highlighted how Lawson and Haus are equally suitable for the roles. “Sitting down with all the seniors on Student Council, it was unclear who would result in a better president,” Jacobsen said. “We’ve got two people who excel in what they do, and they’ve both shown over the past few years that the role of president would be a good role for them.” Jacobsen explained the transition of Student Council’s leadership from a president and vice president to two co-presidents. The decision, according to her, aims to create a balanced and dynamic leadership team for next year. “They’re good friends, and they’ve also been leaders of their class for a long time. They bring two different personalities together to Student Council, and I think they’ll balance each other out well,” Jacobsen said. The Octagon, under the leadership of its student editors-in-chief (EICs) and adviser Andrea Todd, publishes eight issues each school year and operates its website, scdsoctagon.net. EICs are selected based not only on their experience with The Octagon, but also on their communication skills, productivity and ability to collaborate effectively while leading and supporting the staff. Senior co-EICs Zema Nasirov, Anisha Mondal, Eesha Dhawan and Rehan Afzal selected juniors Kate Barnes, Lukas Chung, Jacob Rabe and sophomore Parsiny Nijher to lead The Octagon for the upcoming year. “We considered group chemistry when deciding our EICs for the 2026-27 school year, and the collective four of them have all shown their willingness to do more than what they’re asked,” Nasirov said. “In their respective sections, I would say they’ve all exemplified that they really understand and know how to write or edit stories in each format.” Co-EIC Rabe stressed the importance of being available for other student staffers. “I’d like to let people know that I can take on more work than normal — just something small to make their jobs less stressful,” he said. Eager to start her tenure, co-EIC Barnes plans to strengthen The Octagon by fostering a more collaborative atmosphere. “A good first step would be to ask our staffers what they want to change and what they want to stay the same,” she said. “Their input matters most.” The Medallion staff produces the school’s yearbook by the end of each academic year. Juniors Aziza Halim and Ana Bains will replace seniors Claire Gemmell and Itzel Zamora as co-EICs for the 2026-27 school year. “Aziza has a great presence in the yearbook. She’s creative, dedicated, detail-oriented and super supportive of the student staff,” The Medallion’s adviser, Sarah Zaragoza-Smith, said. “Ana is extremely deadline-oriented, often turning in assignments early. She was on top of everything in a really impressive, mature and responsible way.” Zaragoza-Smith emphasized the balance between the two future EICs. “I think Aziza is an incredible creative force, and Ana is the steadying force that helps everyone stay on track, understand deadlines and work toward meeting them,” Zaragoza-Smith said. “That’s a beautiful balance, and I believe we’ll be tremendously successful next year.” Halim has been involved in yearbook production since her sophomore year, progressing from staff member to assistant editor. She hopes to apply what she has learned from past editors to her role as EIC. “Next year, I want to work closely with Ana to keep everyone on track and make sure we meet deadlines,” Halim said. “Since EICs will have more responsibility reviewing spreads and giving feedback, staying organized will matter a lot. I also want us to choose a theme everyone likes and let people work on spreads they enjoy because that makes the work stronger and helps the whole staff stay motivated.” Looking ahead, Zaragoza-Smith hopes more students will recognize the value of the yearbook and the stories it preserves. “It’s worth it, and dedicating your time to telling the story of the year is really an incredible endeavor,” Zaragoza-Smith said. “I hope more students want to join us in achieving that.”

articles.headline: Leaving teachers reflect on Country Day
articles.body:
Longtime Sacramento Country Day high school teachers Jane Bauman and Richard Day, as well as Director of College Counseling Alicia Perla are leaving Country Day after the 2025-26 school year. Bauman’s position will be filled by Jeff Grant, Day’s by Mika Court and Perla’s by Susan McGuire.

Au Revoir, Monsieur Day High school French teacher Richard Day began his teaching career at Country Day in the spring of 1995. He was fresh out of graduate school from University of California (UC), Davis. He had met the then-lower school French teacher Gerlinde Klauser when she taught a language class at UC Davis. She recommended him for a two to two and a half month substitute position at Country Day. Instantly, he liked working there. “I liked the vibe. I liked the small school. I liked the kids. The students seemed motivated, and the faculty seemed very committed and devoted,” Day said. But after that short stint, he returned to his family in France for two years. When he returned in 1997, Klauser told him about open French teaching positions in both the middle and high schools. He preferred high school. “I had realized that I was not cut out for middle school. I don’t really have the temperament to work with people that age,” he said. He was named the new high school French teacher, which he has remained for 29 years. Day’s favorite memories from his time at Country Day include taking his students to Café Rolle (a now-closed French café on H street), attending the Monterey Jazz Festival with the music students and playing guitar and harmonica in the faculty jazz band (FJC), which included Bob Ratcliff, a math teacher who played piano and a physics teacher who played trumpet and Ratcliff’s friend, a professional drummer. The FJC got gigs in Davis because of Day’s connections there. “We thought, well, this is fun. Why don’t we gig out? So we actually started gigging outside the school,” he said. Day enjoyed the free reign he has had as a teacher. “I’ve liked the freedom, basically, to run my classes the way I want,” he said. But after nearly three decades of l’enseignement du francais, it was finally time for un changement de course. “I want to relax when I have time to do what I want to do while I still can,” he said. But Day isn’t quite ready to disappear. “I do want to stick around, but in a capacity that’s just more relaxed. I’m looking forward to being able to come in and sub and keep my foot in the door, so to speak, without any pressure,” he said. He says that being around kids makes him feel younger and happier, and it provides some sort of escape. “When there are heavy things that are going on in your life, being around kids, for me, has been kind of a break,” he said. Looking to the future, Day wants to slowly move away from substituting. He looks forward to visiting his family in France and having more time pour lui. “I don’t anticipate going back this summer, but I don’t have to wait for the summer anymore. I could go back, pretty much anytime I want,” he said. “To use musical jargon, you know, all in all, it’s been a good gig.”

Et tu, Bauman? High School English teacher Jane Bauman started as a long-term substitute for lower school French in 2003. After substituting twice, a position opened up in high school English. She was originally hired to teach English 9 in 2005. For most of her Country Day tenure, Bauman has been a part-time teacher. She taught three ninth grade English classes until 2012, when she became Director of College Counseling. She worked as a college counselor until 2022. She continued to teach English for 10 more years at the same time, eventually switching to Advanced Placement English. In 2025, Bauman received the High School Faculty Award for the 2024-25 school year. Bauman obtained her undergraduate degree in French literature at UC Santa Cruz. She also has a masters in teaching English as a second language and bilingual education from Georgetown. “UC Santa Cruz had a special kind of approach to education. The emphasis is on students finding their interests and individualizing their study,” she said. UC Santa Cruz didn’t give traditional report cards when she graduated. Instead, they gave long evaluation comments/transcripts, a style which further influences the way she teaches. This style of learning resonated with Bauman and was a large part of her choice to teach at Country Day, rather than another school. “Many aspects of independent education resonate with me: helping students find their voice, helping them tailor their education to what is important to them,” she said. One of her favorite aspects of her work at Country Day was her time as the Director of College Counseling. “As a college counselor, I had some incredible opportunities. Colleges sponsor trips to their campuses for college counselors, and I was invited to see NYU Abu Dhabi,” she said. She later sent a student to NYU Abu Dhabi, and she is still in touch with him to this day. The thing she will miss most? “The intellectual connections with students and colleagues,” she said. What she won't miss at all? “Grading,” she said, calling a stack of ungraded essays “daunting.” Bauman said she purposely assigned essays “of a personal nature” because they were “more interesting to read.” She has a deeper connection to Country Day than just being a teacher. “My daughter [Claire] graduated in 2009, and my son [Jeff] graduated in 2006, so they had the Country Day high school experience,” she said. Her husband, Paul Bauman, also served as an adviser for The Octagon. “Country Day has been in our family and in our life for many, many years,” she said. Bauman looks forward to spending more time traveling and with her husband. “I’ve been here for 23 years, so I'm ready to do something else. I joke around that if I don’t retire, my husband’s going to travel without me,” she said. The Octagon would like to thank Bauman for letting us use her room for class hours and late-night pasteups. Ammar says, “Sorry about the thermostat!”

Perla returning to Portland or Perla’s New Quest Alicia Perla joined Country Day as a college counselor in 2021; she is now the Director of College Counseling. The previous counselor had left at the end of the school year, and Perla filled the position. “I had done some volunteer work with Ms. Bauman and was getting a certification in college counseling, and so they reached out to me to ask if I’d be interested in filling the role,” she said. Perla holds a B.A. from Columbia University, a J.D. from The University of Michigan Law School and a Certificate in College Admission and Career Planning from UC Berkeley. She decided to start college counseling because she enjoys working with students. “I enjoy helping them figure out what kind of next steps in planning out what they want to do,” she said. Perla particularly focuses on underprivileged students and has served on the ScholarMatch board of directors — an organization that helps underprivileged students get into and complete college — since 2021. She also worked towards getting first-generation and lower-income students into college at Country Day. “I really enjoyed helping students without as many resources figure out their college experience as well,” she said. She also helped create the first QuestBridge match ever at Country Day for a student in the class of 2025. QuestBridge is a program that matches students from low-income backgrounds with full four-year scholarships to top colleges, according to the QuestBridge website. Now that her kids are in college, though, she feels ready to move on to her next chapter. Both her daughters — Simone ‘23 and Ceci ‘25 — graduated from Country Day “I’ve always wanted to live in Portland, Oregon. That’s where my sister lives, and I visited a bunch of times. And I thought now would be a good time,” she said. Once she’s in Oregon, she’s going to take some time to settle down and figure out what’s next in terms of college counseling. “I’m not gonna work at a school at this point. I think I would like to do college counseling as an independent college counselor, but I want to try and figure out how to do that in a way that fits my priorities and values,” she said. “I want to make college counseling more accessible to folks who can’t necessarily afford it.”

articles.headline: Freshman Foci: Ashley Lattyak
articles.body:
Ashley Lattyak, ‘25, has completed her first year of college at University of California (UC), Berkeley.

Q: What were your expectations of college before starting at UC Berkeley? A: I think I mostly expected it to be a very big and overwhelming place. Berkeley is a huge school with over 30,000 undergrads, and I was expecting it to be a big transition from how small the Country Day is. It’s very difficult classes, a bunch of different smart people, a big, kind of crazy, overwhelming, chaotic environment. But also, hopefully, a fun and social good balance of work and life. I honestly didn’t know that much about what to expect because I feel like I was definitely a bit nervous and not super clear on expectations of what it would be like.

Q: What would you say you were most nervous about starting college? A: I think I was most nervous about moving to a new place, away from my parents, friends and everything I'd ever known. Having to completely restart, make new friends and adjust to a completely different structure for classes and my day-to-day life.

Q: What surprised you most about UC Berkeley? A: One thing that definitely surprised me is that it doesn't feel nearly as big as I thought it would. I thought I would walk to class and never really run into people I knew; I thought I would feel like a really small person compared to how big the school is. But it honestly feels so much more with the community and a lot smaller than I thought it would be. Every single day I’ll run into multiple people I know, whether that's in a class or just on my walk somewhere. It doesn't feel nearly as separated as I thought it would, and it honestly is a lot less intimidating.

Q: What's the biggest difference between UC Berkeley and Sacramento Country Day? A: So many things are different, but probably the most different thing is just how much more freedom you have. You don't have to wake up at seven to get to school at eight. You can wake up at any time and choose to wake up early and go to the gym or go do a club thing, or just sleep in and then go to bed late. And even on the weekends, you might be doing things that are so different from what you do in high school. Like, it's super common for people to go to San Francisco on the weekends. That freedom to be able to do whatever you want with your schedule, it can be kind of scary because you don't have as much structure.

Q: What are your hardest and easiest classes and what are you currently studying? A: I am double majoring in applied mathematics and economics. My hardest class right now is probably my math class. I'm taking Math 55: Discrete Mathematics. It is just very different from any math I've taken up until this point. The easiest class I take is Music 27: Introduction to Western Music, which is for the arts and literature requirement. I enjoy the class a lot, but it's definitely a lighter workload. We learn about Mozart, Beethoven, Bach and a bunch of romantic Baroque musicians from a few centuries ago.

Q: Are you glad you chose to go to UC Berkeley? A: I genuinely couldn't be happier. I feel like it's the perfect balance of being very strong academically, especially for what I want to study. It has a very good math program with professors and resources that are just incredible. And I've loved the people and all the friends I've made.

Q: What is your favorite part of campus? A: First of all, the buildings themselves are gorgeous. There's a lot of old architecture that's just really pretty. My favorite building is Doe Library, which is an old, sort of Harry Potter style library. I actually fell in love with it on Cal Day last year.

Q: What does your college social life look like? Are you in any school clubs? A: I'm in a sorority, and I love it. It's been an amazing experience and I think it was a really good thing to do because Berkeley is such a big school, and it can kind of seem a bit intimidating at first to make friends and get acclimatized to the culture here. But it’s been a great way to meet so many people and to have some more familiar faces around campus. I am in a club called Undergraduate Women in Economics at Berkeley. It’s for people who are either economics majors or just interested in economics. And it's been great. I’m on the Finance Committee, and we help people guide their career paths and explore different career options.

Q: What’s been the most challenging adjustment? A: Meeting so many people who are just very accomplished in what they want to do and have a very clear idea of what they want to do. But for me, I have a decent idea of what I want to do and I've gained much more of an idea since coming to Berkeley. I knew I probably wanted to do something in finance, but I didn't really have a specific idea beyond that. But I think the people who did know exactly what they wanted to do were a little bit scary for me.

Q: What’s one moment at Berkeley that you’ll never forget? A: One of my favorite weekends from this year was right at the beginning of the second semester back in January. A couple of my friends and I took a little day trip into San Francisco and it was really fun, because I had never left campus to go somewhere a decent distance away with my friends before, and it felt like such a good example of how much freedom we have in college.

Q: What are your plans for the summer? A: I am studying abroad in London as part of Berkeley's global internships program. I'm going there for two months, all of June and July, and I'll be living in an apartment with other Berkeley students who are also doing the program. One part of the program is they also set you up with an internship while you're there. I don't know exactly what that's going to be yet, but I'm hoping it'll be something related to finance, economics, math — my kind of personal academic interests.

Q: What is your advice for the incoming college freshman class? A: College is just a time of so many new experiences, and you should try to do as much as you can. Don't say no to anything. Don't be worried about what other people are going to think, what you've done in the past or be restricted by anything, just do anything that your heart desires. When you're making new friends, be super open to meeting anyone. You might meet your closest friends. And there's so many opportunities to do new things and have new experiences. I think you should just be open to all of it and take advantage of these four years to explore everything you can and gain as many new experiences as you can. articles.headline: Freshman Focus: Cara Shin
articles.body:
Cara Shin, ‘25, attends Pitzer College. She is undecided on her major but plans to pursue economics.

Q: How did you end up choosing Pitzer? A: Honestly, it’s all kind of a blur. I think I had two options, and it was really the location — I thought living in SoCal would be nice. I visited twice before I went there, and I really liked the environment and the people. I think that was the main reason.

Q: What is the environment like at Pitzer? A: It’s very small. I feel like everyone knows everyone here, which I don’t know if that’s a good or bad thing. All the professors are really nice — they’re willing to talk, willing to help. I would say the main takeaway is that it’s very small.

Q: Do you have any thoughts on transferring? A: I do think about that sometimes. Maybe it’s because this is my first year, but I don’t know if Pitzer is where I want to be for the rest of my years at college. It has been growing on me slowly though. The peak of my transfer thoughts were during my winter break. I had left school on a really bad note because I got strep throat and was dealing with other health issues during my finals week. It really affected my performance in school so I left feeling really frustrated and out of place with Pitzer. However, my second semester has been going exponentially better. I’m enjoying my classes, spending more time with friends and overall feeling more at home.

Q: If you were to transfer, where would you be considering? A: I would definitely go to a bigger school, and I have considered applying to all the UCs. School spirit is a big factor that just isn’t really there at Pitzer, because the sports aren’t huge. But also, meeting new people, because Pitzer is so small you just run into the same people all the time. I’m not sure if there is a definitive reason to stay or leave — I think I’ll just have to eventually make that decision later. My perspective on Pitzer has already been positively shifting the longer I am here, so I hope that trend continues.

Q: Are you involved in any extracurricular activities? A: I’m in a couple, and it’s really chill and not much of a commitment. We have a school magazine called “The Outback,” and I’m also in an affinity group for Asian students, PASU, which is an acronym for Pasifika Asian Student Union.

Q: What is your housing situation like? A: I’m in a suite and it’s really nice. I live with one other person, and I share a bathroom with two other people. Most of the other students living on campus are in similar or even better housing situations than mine.

Q: What do you do for fun? A: For fun, I usually go on trips on the weekend. I’m really close to Los Angeles, so, this semester, I’ve gone like every weekend. I like going to Koreatown, but LA as a whole too.

Q: How is the food? A: I have access to all the dining halls of the “Five C’s” (Pitzer College, Pomona College, Scripps College, Harvey Mudd College, Claremont McKenna College), so even though my school is really small, I have seven to choose from. My dining hall is named “McConnell,” but there’s so many others. If you’re not feeling the menu of that day, you can just go to another dining hall — and they’re all really good. I still get tired of the food sometimes, but it is very good and I really appreciate it.

Q: Why did you choose to stay in-state? A: I think I just love California. It was hard to imagine myself on the East Coast, and I’m so used to California weather, so I mostly applied to West Coast schools.

Q: What is Pitzer’s average class size? A: It’s super small, usually 14 or 15, like Country Day classes. Some classes can be up to around 40 people, but that’s like if you’re in a big math class. It also depends, because you can take classes at places like Scripps or Pomona. I can even major at a different school if I want to as long as it’s in the “Five C’s.”

Q: How was the transition from Country Day to Pitzer like? A: I think moving away in general was a huge transition, but classes-wise, it didn’t feel that hard. Last semester was challenging because I didn’t enjoy my classes — there was nothing I was really interested in, and it is relatively hard to get in all the classes you want as a first-year. Additionally, I didn’t realize the classes that I chose would be so writing-heavy, which is definitely not my forte. This semester however, my classes are all economics-related, so I felt better prepared, and they were more enjoyable. Social-wise, it’s a little bit overwhelming for me, because you’re constantly surrounded by everyone — but it’s a good and bad thing. All of your friends are literally down the hall, across the street, and you’re just constantly together.

Q: What is one piece of advice you would like to give to the class of ‘26? A: I would say to focus on your health and bring lots of medicine to college. I’ve gotten sick four times this year, and once one person gets a cold, everyone gets sick.

articles.headline: Entrepreneurship Reborn at Country Day
articles.body:
Is Country Day Out Of Business (Classes)?

What course should young entrepreneurs take in high school? Easy answer: Economics. Advanced Placement Microeconomics (AP Micro) was a straightforward choice for the students interested in business at Sacramento Country Day. Senior Liam Donohue is one such student, so when he was informed that AP Micro had been discontinued while selecting his courses for this year, he had no choice but to find other options. “There are so many people wanting to go into business. I’m going to be double-majoring in Economics and Psychology, so an economics class would obviously help a lot,” Donohue said. AP Micro — a course that “prepares students to think like economists by using principles and models,” according to CollegeBoard — was replaced by Advanced Topics in Human Behavior (AT Human Behavior) in the 2025-26 school year. Donohue signed up. High School math teacher Jo French was hired in the spring of 2022. French replaced a prior teacher, meaning that he needed to fulfill the previous teacher’s course lineup — including AP Micro. Upon starting to teach AP Micro, French realized that the course didn’t live up to its business-based reputation, with the course covering few business skills, with its main focus being how the economic market works. “I think there are certain principles in there that can apply to business, but it’s definitely not a practical, ‘how to get a business going and running,’” he said. French felt a need for high schoolers to learn about people. He proposed a few replacement class ideas for AP Micro — including AP Psychology — ahead of the 2025-26 school year. He was eventually given the opportunity to present an original course curriculum to Head of High School Brooke Wells. French’s idea was AT Human Behavior — a rigorous course that contains a broad examination of how people work beyond what a course like AP Psychology covers. “This was pretty much my personal dream course, my stand on the soapbox, and this is what I think can help our students,” said French. The first semester takes a look at psychology, sociology and behavioral economics. The second semester focuses on problem solving and critical thinking, including a lot about how the brain works and why people do what they do. For the entrepreneurs at Country Day, French’s AT Human Behavior course teaches elements of AP Micro, like behavioral economics. But for business-oriented students, is it a sufficient replacement for AP Micro? “[AT Human Behavior] doesn’t do the same thing as economics would. It has a brief unit on behavioral economics, but [it’s] not micro-specific,” said Donohue. He still believes that Country Day needs a microeconomics or macroeconomics course. “There’s so many people wanting to go into business. Offer a micro or macro class,” said Donohue.

Country Day DECA Builds A Brand

Along with the arrival of the brand-new AT Human Behavior class came new business-related clubs, one of those being the DECA & Entrepreneurship elective. DECA is officially DECA Inc., an acronym that used to stand for Distributive Education Clubs of America, but is now outdated and stands for nothing in particular — a result of the club’s international reach and shift towards Career & Technical Education (CTE). The student-led CTE organization prepares emerging high school and collegiate entrepreneurs around the globe for careers in marketing, finance, hospitality and management. When middle and high school entrepreneurship teacher Brian Hemsworth arrived as a new teacher for the 2025-26 school year, he brought DECA along. At his previous job at the Adelson School in Las Vegas, he served as the full time DECA advisor. Country Day students had the opportunity to start DECA & Entrepreneurship as an elective with Hemsworth. Sophomore Maya Shukla was one of the founding members of the chapter and later grew it to a 14 member class as the chapter’s Vice President of Competition. “It’s an amazing opportunity to get kids real world experience [in business]. It’s really helped my leadership skills, and it’s let me learn more hands on,” she said. DECA offers multiple guest speaker opportunities and a school-based conference called CavCon for on-campus competition experience, run like any other DECA-run conference. Students in DECA also have the chance to contribute to a student-run business. Said business is Country Day DECA’s custom apparel service, Cavaliers & Co. They’ve produced shirts for the homecoming basketball game at Golden 1 Center, the Solar Regatta team, the school auction and more. To customize the apparel, students operate an on-campus heat press, funded by a $4,000 pitch students made to school administrators last fall. Maya Shukla says future Country Day entrepreneurs should “definitely join DECA,” but that there should be more choices. “DECA is the only [business] option, but we need way more. We need a microeconomics class,” she said.

Business Club Swims With Sharks

Another business opportunity for students at Country Day is Business Professionals of America (BPA) that operates within the Business Club. Donohue, who leads the club with senior Gavin Wang, says the meetings are a space for members to get support on various business competitions. “There’s two ways to stand out to universities and colleges in terms of business. Have your own business, which is pretty hard to do, or you can do competitions like the ones in the Business Club,” said Donohue. The club engages in multiple business competitions, most notably BPA, another CTE organization. The BPA program, according to their website, “facilitates students demonstrating their career skills at regional, state and national conferences in more than 90 competitive events.” Sophomore Sid Shukla and freshman Trisha Gandhi will lead the club together next year as co-presidents.

AP Business Not Available at Country Day. Yet.

According to the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), business has grown to become the most popular college major in the United States, with 19% of bachelor’s degrees conferred in 2021-22 being in business. As a result, College Board’s AP program has rolled out a new AP course: AP Business with Personal Finance. A college-level introductory business course in nature, the curriculum delves into “the business disciplines of entrepreneurship, marketing, finance, accounting, and management through real-world business application, case studies, and project-based learning,” according to AP Central, College Board’s AP Website. Sacramento Country Day does not currently plan to offer the new course. French says that AP Business makes sense for students that are interested in starting their own business, and he recommends using high school as an opportunity to develop a well-rounded education. Excelling in a range of subjects — like English for communication and math for financial analysis — is what French believes builds a strong foundation for students looking into business later in their education, namely graduate schools of business. One of French’s former students described majoring in business as being a “specialized generalist.” “I’m all for personal finance. The problem here at Country Day is our size. We have limited resources. If you put in a personal finance course, what are you going to take out? It’s a question of where you allocate your resources at this point,” French said. “It’s a bummer that we’re not offering [AP Business], but I think we just don’t have the teacher for it,” Maya Shukla said. If the course was offered by her senior year in the 2027-28 school year, she says that she would “100% take it.” “Honestly, I think half my grade would.”

articles.headline: No Shame in Community College
articles.body: Sacramento Country Day is a highly academic, (expensive) private college prep school, meaning that the main goal when students graduate is to attend a four-year university directly after high school. Most families send their children here with that intention in mind and consequently are willing to pay a large tuition for that purpose. Therefore, community college is considered to be “off the table.” Right? Wrong. Community college is a shrewd business decision and a prudent option for many Sacramento Country Day students, as they have the opportunity to complete their general education requirements for a fraction of the cost of a four-year university. It’s a great deal. Students then have the opportunity to finish the rest of their education at a four-year university, taking more targeted classes to align with their career goals. Not to mention, they will have a brand new upper division (college) GPA; transfer students have the benefit of a fresh start. Those required courses you were forced to take? Those first two years you may have struggled through academically? Gone. Poof! And higher GPAs up your chance of getting into graduate study, medical, business and law schools. Understandably, many students want the satisfaction of going to a four-year university, and they settle for less preferred schools in order to get that kind of instant gratification. But consider the benefit of waiting for the right school and taking an alternate route in order to get the best education possible. Community colleges, in California specifically, don’t close any doors to higher education for students. In California, six of the ten University of California (UC) schools (UC Davis, UC Merced, UC Irvine, UC Riverside, UC Santa Barbara and UC Santa Cruz) participate in a program called Transfer Admission Guarantee (TAG). This program offers guaranteed admission to California community college transfer students — if they are willing to wait for the opportunity and attend a smaller school as a prerequisite. There are major benefits to this program, as it allows students to save thousands of dollars and gives the guarantee of a great school. Nonetheless, certain limitations are in place for TAG. Students can only apply to one UC with a TAG application. Similarly, they may not be able to pursue certain majors such as computer science, engineering and nursing, due to their selectivity and competition. The general acceptance rate when applying to UC Berkeley as an incoming college freshman applicant is 11.4%, whereas applying to the same school as a community college transfer student (not through the TAG program) increases the acceptance rate to almost 25%. When applying to UCLA as a freshman applicant, the acceptance rate is roughly 9%, whereas the transfer acceptance rate is 23%. These are dramatic increases, more than doubling your chances of admission just by being a transfer. While the transfer rate from community college to UC Berkeley is 25%, the transfer rate between UCs is 2%. Therefore, if you commit to a UC that you don’t really want to attend, you are essentially stuck there. Committing to community college makes your chance of getting into your dream UC much more attainable. The average California in-state community college tuition is $1,390 per year, though many community college students are eligible for federal and state grants. California community colleges have the lowest average tuition out of all of the states. The average tuition (without financial aid) to a UC is $15,588 per year. However, the majority of students whose families income is between $0 - $100,000 a year don’t pay any tuition at all. The amount of grant and scholarship money received by the average (eligible) student is $22,000. This covers full tuition. According to EducationWeek, 44% of college students want to attend graduate school as of 2014. And graduate school is not cheap. Community college could be a strategic move for many students who are on this path. For example, if you are an aspiring medical doctor, where you earned your undergraduate degree is largely irrelevant compared to your test scores. Could it be better to save the money you would spend on a top 20 college and spend it on a top 20 medical school? Most driven students will thrive in community college and will have better GPAs than if they attend prestigious schools with grade deflation (academic policy/curve that limits how many students can get top grades). This higher GPA and more unique story may benefit them in the long run. Community college is also perfect for students who aren’t ready to go to college yet, want a slower transition into moving away from home or need to stay back to care for their families. College life isn’t for everyone immediately after high school. Similarly, if you pick a school that isn’t among your top choices and commit there, you risk unhappiness. According to the National Library of Medicine (NLM), student happiness is dependent on strong academic performance, adequate sleep and loving relationships. Notably, nowhere in this list was the school’s prestige mentioned. 60% of college students already report feeling high levels of stress. Attending a top 20 school also means being a part of the top 20 most competitive college environments. Pressure is very high. At the end of the day, the student matters more than the school. The student should choose the school — not the other way around. Forcing yourself towards the instant gratification of attending a four-year college instead of the embarrassment surrounding community college is not worth it. You decide how good a school is by making the most of the resources it provides you and by becoming the best student you can with these resources. There is extreme stress and anxiety placed upon students to apply to and attend universities and colleges. While you should always be giving school all that you can, know that getting into a top school immediately out of high school is not the be-all and end-all of your academic and professional career. Don’t sacrifice your happiness and well-being and spend (hundreds of) thousands of (your parents’) hard-earned dollars because you are afraid that someone will judge your work ethic and initial level of success based on your college commitment.
