articles.headline: Advice column
articles.body:
This advice column responds to questions shared by Sacramento Country Day students anonymously. To submit, send a question to the Google Form sent out on April 26. Responses are not guaranteed, but all submissions are welcome.

My friend started to hang out with this person from another school, and I don’t trust them. What am I supposed to do if I disapprove of my friend’s dating life?

As their friend, you’re in a unique position: tell them about your concerns, and they might listen, but there’s always the chance that saying something will hurt your friendship. And that’s the source of the conflict, isn’t it? Assuming that your friend really enjoys spending time with this person, pointing out flaws in their relationship could wound them deeply — especially if this criticism is coming from you, a friend that they trust. But you have to decide what matters more: your friend’s well-being, or your relationship with them. I would hope the answer is obvious. If you have reasons to be genuinely concerned, then your friend’s safety needs to come first; you need to come clean and tell them what you think. Best-case scenario? You give your friend a much-deserved wake up call. If you believe that this person does not have your friend’s best interests at heart — maybe based off of this person’s behavior in the past — then tell them so. Lay out the evidence you have against them, and make your case, no baseless accusations allowed. And then: let your friend decide. It may be hard, but you need to trust their judgement. After you present to them the facts, they should choose their own path forward. Maybe they decide to stop dating this person, maybe they assure you that they have everything under control. Respect their choice. There’s a fine line between concern and manipulation — don’t cross it. But your friend could also be lying to you, or maybe themselves. And that brings us to the worst-cast scenario: your friend is in serious trouble and needs help. Maybe you suspect that they’re suffering from gaslighting, emotional or even physical abuse at the hands of this untrustworthy person. How do you tell for sure, though, if they swear that they’re fine? Just ask yourself: is this the same friend that you knew before they met this untrustworthy person? Chances are, if your friend is acting out of the ordinary, becoming withdrawn or overly anxious, their relationship could be the cause. The next step is to get an adult involved. Talk to a school counselor or a trusted adult if you believe that your friend is in danger. They can give you guidance about what to do next — maybe convince your friend to talk to the school counselor. Don’t take this next step alone, though: you aren’t impartial, and you don’t always know what’s best for your friend. Yes, both the best-case scenario and worst-case scenario could lead to a rift forming between you and your friend; it’s hard to take criticism about relationships, even if you mean well. But a healthy friendship, founded on trust and respect, will bounce back — especially if you have their best interests at heart.

My parents are always getting mad at me when I get anything less than an A and telling me that I need to start worrying about college. I’m a freshman. What should I do?

It’s hard to say no to parents. They tell you to get an A, you try to get an A. They tell you to worry about college, you start worrying about college. That’s how it is, if you’ve never been told to prioritize anything different. I’m here to tell you to prioritize something different: your happiness. Your parents mean well, and they want you to succeed, but perfection is not success, and vice versa. You should do work that you are proud of, whatever that means for you — whether that means maintaining As and Bs in classes or pursuing a topic you’re truly interested in, which is what I suggest underclassmen should focus on. Doing work that you are passionate about, instead of focusing on perfection, isn’t self-indulgence; what your parents may not realize is that good test scores don’t get you into college. More often than not, passion projects and unique interests stand out to admission officers more than anything else. And this is the angle you could use to convince your parents to, for once, let up on you. It’s easy to understand that perfection is not sustainable, nor is it the best way to achieve your goals, but it’s not so easy to make your parents understand. You have to appeal to both their logic and their emotions if you want to change their mind. First, explain the toll that maintaining perfect grades is having on you. You might be constantly stressed, not getting enough sleep or not eating enough. Your parents care about your well-being, and they don’t want you to suffer. Then, lay out the logical benefits that focusing more on the quality of your work would have, rather than focusing on the amount of As you have. Spending more time on pursuing your interests not only relieves stress, it rounds out your (distant) college application. If your parents are demanding about your grades and academics, this is the language they will likely respond to the most. Beyond that, do what you want to do. Draw, paint, research niche topics, and don’t worry so much about what exact number your GPA is.

articles.headline: My Angle: Eating Disorders are Back
articles.body:
Disclaimer: the content in this article contains sensitive topics relating to eating disorders and self-harm.

I used to walk into my middle school bathroom and hear the sound of a girl trying to throw up her lunch at least once per month. The sickness was spreading at my school. Some of my friends told me that they weren’t hungry, that they just didn’t feel like eating lunch. They assured me that they would just eat as soon as they got home. For a few weeks I believed them. Then I noticed they were getting smaller and smaller. Not just that, but they would always talk about the way they looked. “Ugh, I feel so fat,” wasn’t an uncommon thing to hear at my lunch table. I knew that something was wrong, but I didn’t know what to do. I knew that if I said anything, they wouldn’t stop, they would just hide it. Anorexia nervosa is one of the most common eating disorders. According to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-V), anorexia is characterized by persistent restriction of food intake, an intense fear of gaining weight and an intense focus on body weight. Anorexia isn’t the only eating disorder. There are a whole host that the DSM-V recognizes, including bulimia, which involves cycles of eating large amounts (or sometimes normal amounts) of food and then throwing it up. Eating disorders as a whole are characterized by an obsession with body image and a large amount of one’s thoughts being consumed by food and weight. The idolization of the “heroin chic” — a sickly, ultra-thin body — never went away, it just got quieter. In the 2000s, like in much of modern history, skinny was in. Celebrities got bombarded with headlines calling them overweight if they even had a little visible fat. Heat magazine’s May 2007 issue had the words “Posh puts weight on” in big bold red letters on the cover. Star magazine had an issue where the cover read “Jessica’s Diet Disaster” and “Stuck at 178 pounds.” Kate Winslet was famously nicknamed “Kate Weighs-a-lot,” during the filming for “Titanic” by the director of the film. Then, around 2010, “body positivity” was starting to trend. Instagram was popular, and there was a wave of bloggers pushing radical acceptance of every size. Of course, that didn’t mean being skinny was out — the majority of people you saw on TV were always skinny — but rather, more diverse bodies were being accepted. Major companies like Dove even began running ads with plus-sized models. By 2019, it really seemed like we were moving towards a direction of acceptance for bigger bodies. Fashion magazines were long dead, and your media diet now consisted less of headlines about weight and more of posts about loving your body. But then, COVID lockdowns began, and everyone was stuck at home with nothing but an internet connection and their own thoughts. By 2021, body dissatisfaction rates were up dramatically, according to a study in the International Journal of Eating Disorders. Consuming short-form video content, especially dieting content, was linked to decreased body appreciation and increased body dissatisfaction. Then, on June 4, 2021, Wegovy — a GLP-1 injection originally developed as a treatment for diabetics — got approved as a weight-loss drug. Being skinny was more accessible than ever — assuming that you had the financial means to pay the, on average, $1,350 per month. Every red carpet, you saw more and more celebrities getting thinner and thinner. Body positivity influencers suddenly lost weight extremely rapidly and told their audience that it was just exercise and diet. Everywhere you looked, skinny was back. Not everyone could afford the hefty price tag that came with a GLP-1, so a cheaper solution arose: not eating. In the past decade alone, eating disorder rates have doubled, from 3.5% to 7.8%. This led to, or maybe is because of, the rise of “Skinnytok,” seemingly the successor to 2000’s pro-anorexia blogs and magazines. Skinnytok is a community of mostly women who encourage each other to lose weight and share dieting tips. But it can quickly become a pro-eating disorder. One TikTok creator, who had previously only posted about music, made a post in January 2026 asking for weight loss tips. By March, they were posting about eating zero to one meals per day. I’ve seen it happen to so many people around me, proving that falling into disordered eating is easy. First, they start on a healthy diet. Calorie deficit and working out, but they’re still eating an adequate amount. The pounds are falling and people tell them they look great. But then they hit a plateau, and they’re not losing weight anymore, so they eat even less. That works for a while, until eventually they hit another plateau, so they cut the amount of calories they’re eating again. This keeps happening; they eat less and less, and eventually it’s taken over their whole life. What might be the worst part is that they don’t actually know how they look. They know exactly what the number on the scale is, but not what they look like; this is called body dysmorphia. They just know that you’re not skinny enough. The fact that every other post on your TikTok For You page romanticizes the feeling of hunger, or tells you that skinny is never skinny enough, only feeds their beliefs. At first, nobody around them sees it as an issue. Other people see “discipline” as so many of these pro-anorexia pages have put it. They get compliments and praise; society rewards people in those early stages. When their friends do see it, it’s hard to say anything. “You look great,” is easy to say; “I’m worried about you” isn’t. So they don’t stop. The silence is part of the problem. But eating disorders are not an individual failure to “see your own beauty,” they are the natural result of a system. A system that is only bolstered by the fact that social media platforms, despite their surface-level safeguards, push harmful content. Outrage, aspiration and apparently hunger all drive engagement online. The Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) found that on average, new TikTok accounts, whose age was set at 13 years old, were being served videos about eating disorders within 8 minutes. Not only were they being fed this content immediately, but also constantly, about every 23 seconds. Platforms like TikTok and Instagram all have filters that prevent words like “eating disorder,” “starving,” and “calorie,” but enforcement is inconsistent at best, and people often find their ways around the filters. X, previously known as Twitter, has no filters for eating disorder content at all. And it’s not just young girls who are having unrealistic standards pushed on them; now it’s everyone. Recently, a survey showed that 23% of men rarely or never feel satisfied with their bodies. The gap between gender body image issues is closing, but not in the way we hoped. Meanwhile, the Ozempic (GLP-1) conversation has made it so much easier to talk about people’s bodies, without actually addressing the root cause. Celebrities who lose a significant amount of weight immediately get hundreds of posts about how they’ve taken Ozempic. Additional posts analyze their facial features to see if they’ve got the sunken eyes, hollowed cheeks and sagging skin that comes with rapid, dramatic weight loss, which they call “Ozempic face.” All the while, each celebrity’s PR team is telling everyone that it’s just a lifestyle change, and they’ve been simply eating more vegetables. All of that just tells the rest of us that we, too, can look exactly like them if only we just tried hard enough. When the “how” is never really discussed, all weight loss starts to look the same. And, when your body is the enemy, any method seems worth it. According to Eating Disorder Hope, an advocacy nonprofit group, anorexia has the highest mortality rate out of any mental illness, 10% within 10 years of onset, 20% within 20 years. This is not a niche fact. Rather, it paints a picture of something that has devastated thousands of people, something that current cultural trends are only making worse. Nonetheless, being more aware doesn’t mean diagnosing everyone around you, but it does mean you might have to sit with some discomfort. It means paying attention to the people around you — not their bodies, but them. Learn to treat your body as neutral, not an ornament to be admired or admonished depending on the number on the scale. If you are worried about someone else or yourself, the National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA) provides free, low-cost resources and treatments for people with eating disorders. NEDA also provides guidance and support for people with patterns of disordered eating: symptoms that are unhealthy but do not fit enough criteria to be diagnosed as an eating disorder.

articles.headline: We're Not Disengaged - You're Not Listening
articles.body: The following is an award-winning entrant in the Journalism Education Association’s National Student Media Contests — this one for commentary writing. Students were provided with a prompt and given 120 minutes to complete their response. Sophomore Sid Shukla’s opinion essay was one of two pieces to be given the highest ranking — “Superior.” Judges described Shukla’s commentary as “concise” and “powerful,” “with a strong, clear voice.” As the United States approaches its 250th anniversary, I keep hearing the same thing: young people are disengaged from civic life. We don’t vote enough. We don’t pay attention. We don’t care. The problem isn’t that my generation is disengaged — it’s that democracy often feels disconnected from us. The cause of that disconnect isn’t apathy — it’s structural. Most high school students are expected to care about political decisions they have no direct role in shaping. We’re told to stay informed, form opinions and think critically. Yet, we can’t vote. We rarely see people even nearly our age represented, and almost never feel like our voices change anything. Over time, this creates distance. It’s hard to stay engaged with a system that treats you as a future participant, not a current one. Schools unintentionally reinforce this gap. Civic education often focuses on memorizing how governments work instead of showing how to participate in it. We learn about branches and amendments, but not how to engage with local leaders or create change in our own community. Participation becomes theoretical instead of real. The solution isn’t telling students to care more — it’s giving them a reason to. Schools should create opportunities for real engagement, like student-led initiatives or direct engagement with local decision-makers. At the same time, adults need to recognize that civic participation has evolved. My generation engages through social media, community action and issue-based movements. These aren’t distractions — they’re legitimate forms of civic engagement. As the country celebrates 250 years of democracy, the question isn’t whether young people will participate — it’s whether democracy is willing to change enough to include them. Because we’re already here. And we have a lot to say. The real issue is whether anyone is ready to listen.

articles.headline: Starbucks Summer Menu Review
articles.body:
The number one coffee chain in the world, Starbucks, debuted their new 2026 summer menu on May 12. Seasonal menus drive up foot-traffic and revenue by creating an urgency for customers to purchase products under a limited-time offer. At Starbucks, the year-round seasonal menus have become an integral part of their marketing strategy — helping to keep customers engaged and excited all year long. I am a self-proclaimed “casual Starbucks fan.” I get Starbucks anywhere from about one to three times a month, and almost always, my orders are from the seasonal menus. The big hits for this year’s summer menu include variations of the new Tropical Butterfly Drink and the two horchata flavored drinks. DISCLAIMER: I have a picky sweet tooth; one that appreciates a certain balance between sickly and saccharine. Thus, the drinks I like may be partial to that.

Tropical Butterfly Drink

This drink is supposed to feel like a summer paradise. A blend of passionfruit, guava and pineapple flavors is complimented by pineapple-mango popping boba and creamy coconut milk. With a butterfly pea infusion, the drink is very pretty, flaunting lavender, pink and orange hues. However, I was rather disappointed when I found out that the butterfly pea was just for show and wouldn’t provide any actual flavoring. Upon first taste, the Tropical Butterfly Drink reminded me a lot of the Pink Drink, except with tart flavors. (The Pink Drink is a very popular drink at Starbucks made of a strawberry acai base along with passionfruit flavors and coconut milk.) You can really taste the sultry fruit blend from the drink itself and the bits of pineapple-mango flavor bursting in your mouth as you sip into the drink. The drink was amazing, and right away, I knew that I would definitely continue ordering this in the future. 4.5/5

Tropical Butterfly Lemonade Refresher

This refresher is a variation of the Tropical Butterfly Drink, but while they share the same foundational base, the Tropical Butterfly Lemonade Refresher replaces the coconut milk with lemonade. Admittedly, the Tropical Butterfly Lemonade Refresher is better-looking, with sharper and more vibrant colors. The drink truly looked like a summer day came early, but as I took my first sip, it became clear that I had set my expectations too high. Switching out the coconut milk for lemonade was a terrible decision. In fact, it ruined the whole drink for me. On paper, it sounds like a great idea, but my taste buds could not disagree more. The sheer amount of sweetness in the lemonade threw me off immediately. And I have a sweet tooth! Instead of feeling refreshed, I was hit with a sharp, pungent taste of sugar and lemon. It tasted rather artificial as well, like a sour candy, leaving me extremely disappointed. 1.5/5

Iced Horchata Shaken Espresso This drink has a combination of vanilla, cinnamon and rice notes with a blonde espresso roast and oat milk. As someone who isn’t a huge fan of coffee (or bitter flavors in general) this drink truly exceeded my expectations. Right away, I could taste a nutty cinnamon flavor — paired with the creamy oat milk. The horchata was definitely there, and it felt like just the right amount. The flavors felt quite unique, the texture was very silky, and it was my first time trying horchata with coffee. Although it is iced, it feels cozy and smooth — a great combination, which I would highly recommend to all coffee/espresso lovers. The drink itself was quite bitter, and I couldn’t really taste much sweetness to it. As it isn’t sweet enough for my preference, I would not buy it again. For those who do enjoy non-sweet drinks, the Iced Horchata Shaken Espresso would be very enjoyable. 3/5

Horchata Frappuccino This is similar to the Iced Horchata Shaken Espresso — but slightly sweeter and more flat. With whipped cream and cinnamon powder sprinkled on top, the drink looks like any generic frappuccino, but it really is way more than that. Oftentimes, I find frappuccinos from Starbucks overly sweet — making me feel more grossed-out and unhealthy rather than happy and satisfied. This drink, however, really amazed me. It’s definitely sweet, yet it has a great balance. You can still taste the slight bitterness from the coffee, and the oatmilk really compliments the flavor. I would absolutely recommend this drink to anyone — with one small tweak: get it without the whipped cream on top. The horchata is there as well; however, compared to the Iced Horchata Shaken Espresso, the flavors feel rather muted. This is in part due to the whipped cream, which adds fluffiness, but takes away from the flavor of the drink. Despite my dislike for Starbucks frappuccinos, the Horchata Frappuccino is a great drink. It is a perfect combination of flavors — not too simple, but not overly complicated either. In fact, it is probably my favorite out of all the drinks in this year’s summer menu. 4.5/5

articles.headline: Creme Coffee Review
articles.body:
Nobody at Crème Coffee seems to be there just for coffee. From friends posing in front of the mirrors to chatty, just off-shift firefighters, this new downtown spot feels like the whole city gathered briefly under one roof. Crème Coffee held its grand opening in downtown Sacramento, in February. According to their website, cremecoffee.com, the cafe draws inspiration from Parisian cafe culture and Italian espresso traditions. Inside, it features a clean, minimalist aesthetic with light colors, marble tables and simple seating that gives it a quietly luxurious feel. Its sign on the wall — “crème de la crème” — is a French idiom for “best of the best.” The cafe serves espresso and brewed coffee, matcha, tea beverages and locally baked pastries. According to the business’s description on Yelp, drinks are prepared using an Italian espresso machine, house-made syrups and beans sourced from specific regions for their quality and flavor. The website claims they serve “Sacramento’s best coffee,” adding a stated goal of making customers “feel welcomed, valued, and treated with every sip.” The advertisement and strong public reviews set my expectations high, creating a standard that each drink had to meet. But only some lived up to that standard.

Crème Matcha Latte - $7.50 As an admittedly self-proclaimed ‘professional’ matcha enthusiast and home-based recreational barista, I can confidently say that the crème matcha latte meets my expectations. This popular drink features a clean, minimalistic look that perfectly matches the cafe’s relaxed vibe. A light sprinkle of matcha powder on the side added an elegant touch. Refreshing and ideal for summer, its light-green color pleases the eye like a poem created in spring. At first glance, the latte resembled a scoop of matcha ice cream more than just a standard beverage. Every matcha should deliver perfect creaminess with little to no bitterness. This drink succeeds with its extremely rich and vegetal flavor. The mellow matcha stays sweet, bold and far from watered-down. It blends Asian and European influences, marrying the earthy matcha with creamy milk almost to perfection. The flavor does not hit all at once. Instead, it strikes a perfect balance — neither overwhelmingly strong nor tasteless. Even from a distance, the delicate scent of spring breezed through. It’s grassy, fresh and deeply relaxing, leaving a lasting impression of silky matcha at its finest. If you want an excellent introduction to the possibilities of matcha, order this crème matcha latte. - 5/5

Crème Latte - $7.50

Upon first taste, it felt as if someone with an extremely bold personality got up in my face. Already not a huge coffee fan, I ordered this signature drink hoping it would finally convert me (spoiler alert: it did not). Without stirring, bitter caramel storms in immediately — two words that should never share a sentence. The cream is completely missing, buried under a cloying wave of sugar. The flavors clash hard: burnt coffee fighting against overly sweet milk. It tastes like they tried to hide the charred bitterness by simply adding cream. There’s no pleasant aftertaste that invites me to revisit. After stirring, it improves slightly as the flavors blend, but the heavy cream is still overwhelming. It’s almost oleaginous enough to cause a headache. The drink does earn points for appearance, though. The clear, distinct layers are genuinely impressive. Cream swirls gently through the warm beige and brown tones, creating a cozy marbling effect that feels comforting and homemade (before you stir it, of course). Looks-wise? Impressive. Taste-wise? Hard pass. - 1/5

Raspberry Hibiscus Tea - $4.50 Tea, or pink-tinted water? This drink is a textbook case of striking looks over any real personality. When I asked for tea recommendations, the tea-rista raved about its “sweet, floral character when blended with vanilla.” I ordered it exactly as described. One sip later, I seriously doubted any vanilla had ever met this cup. Instead of warmth and depth, it tasted like plain water — as if the hibiscus and raspberry had both called in sick. Hibiscus tea should be vibrant and berry-like: pleasantly tart with a subtle sweetness. This version delivered none of that. It arrived severely watered down, with zero noticeable sourness or gentle sweetness. The color is undeniably beautiful — a vibrant pink that almost makes you feel guilty for disliking it. But looks are nothing without taste. In the end, this raspberry hibiscus tea feels like something a beginner whipped up at home: good intentions, but sadly lacking the depth and balance. - 2/5

In a world where everything seems to be advancing toward intricacy and modernism, Crème Coffee’s concept slows life to the basics — without making it basic. Their simple yet classic layout is magnetic; it’s a place that subtly, subconsciously coaxes you to fix your posture to match the poised manner of the architectures. Amid marble surfaces and soft light echoes carefree Parisian mornings: slow unwinding with calm greetings and gentle clinks of cups. The minimalistic European vibe is conspicuous, yet the serenity is often disrupted by the constant loud noise of a full room. Do not expect to get much work done at Crème Coffee unless you bring top-tier headphones. The drinks are a similar story of uneven delivery. The crème matcha latte stands out as rich, vegetal and beautifully balanced, easily the highlight. In contrast, the Crème Latte was bitter-sweet chaos, while the Raspberry Hibiscus Tea feels like a decoration where hibiscus and raspberry have entered their minimalist era (nice job hitting your theme, I guess). While I respect the confidence, hanging “crème de la crème” on the wall might be a stretch. Right now, I can only think of one drink which belongs in that conversation.

articles.headline: BULLY Review
articles.body:
Kanye West — never a stranger to controversy — dropped his latest studio album “BULLY,” on March 28. West, now known as “Ye,” rose to prominence as a producer for artists such as Jay-Z before launching his groundbreaking solo career in 2004 — his debut album “The College Dropout” won a Grammy for Best Rap Album. Ye has built a reputation on innovation and meticulous production. His past work often balanced experimentation with structure, creating projects that felt both ambitious and fully realized. “BULLY,” however, leans heavily on sampling and minimalistic structure, leaving it sounding incomplete and lacking in effort overall. The design is consistent with Ye’s former aesthetic choices: Tracks are in all-caps, signalling drama, boldness, and the importance of his message. It’s in your face. Throughout this so-called redemption album, two songs stood out to me: an attempt to deliver impact and an unfinished cacophony of sound.

“FATHER” Featuring rapper Travis Scott, “FATHER” feels like a track with ambition but no cohesion. Lyrically, this track is built around themes of legacy, identity and personal reflection. But these concepts feel underdeveloped — as if they were presented in pieces rather than fully shaped ideas. He sings: “Bye-bye to my old self / Wake up to the new me.” It’s a hook that highlights leaving his old self behind and abandoning a chaotic past for a more mentally stable life, but that idea quickly becomes muddled by lyrics that focus less on growth and more about wealth and status. In lines such as “I used to be on Worldstar / Now I’m making Newsweek / I used to hang on the 9 / Now I bought two streets,” the singer seems caught between self-reflection and self-glorification. Frenzied, uneven production stood out to me — it created a sense of a song building towards something big — yet every time it got close, it pulled back, leaving the listener frustrated and unsatisfied. Travis Scott adds texture and energy, but even then, it doesn’t fully stabilize the track’s shifting direction. I get what the song was aiming for thematically, but the execution was too fragmented for me to connect. By the end, it left me with uncertainty rather than impact; the ideas were present but never tied together. Or to use “therapese”? Never processed. ⅖

“BULLY” “BULLY.” As the title track and supposed centerpiece of the album, it finishes as a missed opportunity rather than a defined statement. Meant to be the track that anchors the project’s themes, it carries expectations going in, but the final result feels rudimentary and messy. In this song, Ye describes a desire to “beat somebody up / Like a bully.” He uses this line as a thinly-veiled metaphor for the aggressive public persona that has defined much of his recent career. The issue is that the metaphor feels almost too simplistic for the weight of his recent actions. Rather than directly confronting the damage his behavior has caused? Ye reduces it to broad statements about anger and insecurity. He raps: “They get mad at me for livin' out my fantasies / All the castles in the sky comе down crashin' every time I spеak my mind.” The production comes across as disconnected rather than intentional. Instead of building towards a clear progression, the track shifts direction without purpose, giving it a disjointed quality. It’s a lazy effort. Rather than feeling like a deliberate centerpiece, it comes across as something that was left in a rough state, without the care or completion you’d expect for the title track. ⅕

REDEMPTION OR REDUCTION? If “BULLY” is intended as a redemption album, it doesn’t achieve that goal. Rather than delivering a clear reset or a convincing return to form, it largely leans towards inconsistency rather than reinvention, with ideas that feel only partially developed. Instead of reframing his artistic direction, Ye produced an album that never quite settles into a clear identity. That said, there are brief moments where the “old” (Kan)Ye emerges, reminding us that he still exists . . . but then he disappears again. Critics have noticed, pointing to moments on “BULLY” as a return to his signature “chipmunk soul.” Those brief flashes suggest the level of precision that defined his strongest works, but appear too sporadically to signal a true comeback.

Overall score: 1.5/5

articles.headline: Drake's Iceman Freezes the World
articles.body:
“Iceman” is the ninth full length album from Canadian singer, songwriter and rapper Aubrey Graham (known by the stage name Drake). Released on May 15, “Iceman” allows Drake to return to his rap-focused self. It is reminiscent of his studio album, 2013’s “Nothing Was The Same” — it has a lot less of the melodic and heartbroken Drake that fans have gotten used to over the past few years. “Iceman” has a very clear central theme running through it. Almost every track deals with the fallout from his 2024 beef with Kendrick Lamar. As such, Drake addresses betrayal and loyalty throughout the entire album. Drake narrates about former friends who switched sides, industry figures who turned their backs on him and rivals who he feels have been given too much credit for their work. Accompanying Drake across the 18 tracks is a solid list of features including the rappers Future, Quavo, Molly Santana and 21 Savage. With a feature list this stacked (and beef to be settled), I was anxious about what I knew would not be a “chill” trip.

“Whisper My Name” The third track, “Whisper My Name,” is my favorite off of this project. The beat is stark and minimal, with a digital pulse running underneath, giving Drake a lot of room to work with. It’s a smart production choice. Drake’s bars are some of the sharpest on the album, with punctuating lines like “I heard what you said to lil’ bro about me” and “when you run into the Iceman, what you gon’ do except freeze?” The combination hits hard — and feels personal. The chorus is incredibly catchy, with Drake referencing his Coachella headline set and hinting at a Rolling Loud performance, making it a memorable hook. This song also stands out because it has no features, leaving Drake to hold it down completely on his own, a solo moment among busier tracks. Rating: 5/5

“Ran to Atlanta” (feat. Future and Molly Santana) “Ran to Atlanta,” the fifth track, is one of my favorite songs on “Iceman.” The reunion between Drake and Future alone made “Run To Atlanta” one of the most anticipated on the album. Future kicks things off with his signature hazy delivery in a line about partying in Turks and Caicos so long he lost track of what day it was. The vibe energizes, excites and intrigues from the start. Drake’s chorus is smooth, his lyrics framing Atlanta as a witness to his whole career, calling out Future and 21 Savage (another rapper) as people who can vouch for his “run.” Molly Santana’s verse in the second half of the song is a pleasant surprise, with her “Molly Santana new Hannah Montana” line already being one of the most talked about on the entire album. She solidly holds her own next to two of the biggest names in rap. The track loses a bit of momentum toward the end, and I feel like a slightly tighter edit would have made it even better than it already is. Rating: 4/5

“Make Them Remember” The fourteenth track, “Make Them Remember,” is the most lyrically impressive song on this album. Nothing else comes close. The production is bare, simple and controlled, with Drake’s producers giving him all the space he needs to do what he does best, which is rap. Drake performs again with focus and intention. Drake’s verses are genuinely remarkable here, and the lyrics he’s belting out? Wow. He takes shots at LeBron James, Lucian Grainge and Kendrick Lamar all in the span of one track. The line “I’m the golden goose, shakin’ things up at Lucian’s house,” shows Drake’s confidence of being the most valuable artist on the label. It’s one of the best lines on the whole album. The track runs a little long (5:23), with some sections that drag in contrast to the sharpness of other work. In areas like these, a tighter edit would have made this the definitive song on “Iceman” without a doubt. Rating: 4/5

Overall, “Iceman” locks in, with the quality of the tracks consistent throughout, separating it from a lot of Drake’s recent work. Most songs hook my attention and rarely let me down. Drake has been more prolific over the course of his career (various albums such as “Views” and “Take Care” have 20+ tracks), but 18 feels like the right amount here. Almost every song serves a purpose — and contributes to the theme of the album — in a way previously (over) hyped albums do not (“For All The Dogs” comes to mind). “Iceman” is the sharpest Drake has sounded in years. I predict it will hold up over time.

articles.headline: No MLB Season 2027
articles.body: To many, an entire summer without one of America's most beloved sports is absurd. After decades of baseball, Major League Baseball (MLB) could be taking its full season off. The combination of labor disputes and the desire for player salary caps has led to rumors of a cancellation of the 2027 season. The MLB has had its fair share of labor disputes and postponed seasons. Most notably, it happened in 1994, where players stayed on strike for a total of 232 days. The reason? Salary caps on players — a problem that still persists in 2026. A salary cap is a limitation or restriction on the amount of money a player can be paid through their contracts. These days, a star player like Shohei Ohtani is paid $125 million from off the field endorsements alone — a salary that is 62 times what he gets paid by the Los Angeles Dodgers, according to the MLB. MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred, alongside the owners of the New York Mets, New York Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies, pushed for the addition of salary caps for players. In 2023, Manfred appeared on The New York Post’s ‘The Show’ podcast where he openly talked about salary caps and his ideas for the future of the league regarding them. “There are arguably five major professional sports in North America. Four of them have one system. One of them has a different system. I’m sort of a believer in the idea that the majority eventually gets it right,” Manfred said. This is much to the displeasure of the Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) and its former director, Tony Clark (who was replaced by Bruce Meyer in February 2026). Clark has shown his distaste for salary caps, turning down the idea every time Manfred and the team owners bring it up. One thing he made very clear was that he believes that a salary cap is a huge limitation on player value. If this decision is implemented, there is no doubt that players will not be happy. This is apparent in Phillies star Bryce Harper, who cursed out Manfred when discussing the topic. While an entire season will undoubtedly leave its mark on the players, it might just hit the fans just as hard. Junior Justin Lawson, an L.A. Dodgers fan, has been following the MLB more closely in recent years. So much so, that a summer without baseball seems unbearable to him. “There’s no basketball during the summer … there’s no football, there's no hockey. You need something to watch. And look, I’m more of a football, basketball guy, but in recent years, baseball is starting to become relevant in my life and on the TVs in my house,” he said “[Sacramento] just got a team that’s only here for a certain amount of years … Sacramento deserves a team, so we want to take advantage of [the team] while they’re here. And I don’t want it to be shut down by some lockdown or lockout,” he added Lawson hopes the players and the MLB find a solution to this problem soon, because the idea of people losing their jobs for a season is absurd to him. Sophomore and San Francisco Giants fan Sean Whited’s day-to-day routine would change quite a bit with the absence of a season. “Most of the time during a lot of my free time, I like to check what the scores are of each game. I just love to watch [baseball] if I don’t have anything to do in the evenings. I don’t know what I would do without it,” he said. Whited remains hopeful that players and owners can come to a conclusion soon so that baseball can continue to be enjoyed by everyone. Sophomore Taber Livesey, who has been playing and following baseball since he was 5 years old, spoke about what he believes should be next for players. “I think it would affect a lot of people who’ve been fans longer than me more than it would affect me in 2027,” he said. Livesey sees the salary caps as a positive solution to an absurd and unfair advantage for other teams. “Owners spending this much money on players is kind of out of hand. Owners have been spending over 700 million on players, which is absurd to hear because just a few years ago, that would have been insane,” Livesey said. “I think it’s unfair for the sport and the fans, because their team wouldn’t be winning a lot without lots of money,” Whited said. Whited also believes that a salary cap might be the league’s best interest, and hopes that everyone can come to a solution soon. “If there’s no salary cap, it might look like what we’re probably seeing with the Dodgers, where they’re getting all the best players because they’re offering them the most money, with no cap at all. I do think to make things fair throughout the season, salary caps do sound like a good idea,” he said. Conversely, Lawson believes that players should be paid a bare minimum for their services. “There needs to be a salary floor … Part of what separates baseball from the three other major leagues is that the other leagues have salary caps. I think that you won’t realize how rich owners actually are, and that there are minority owners that can also fund these and they’re not willing to, like the Dodgers,” he said MLB seasons being postponed aren’t anything new, from the shortened season in 2020 to the 10 day strike in 1972. The loss of a season would without a doubt impact many people’s lives. Unfortunately, the only thing fans can do at this point is hope that the players and the league will reach a conclusion soon so that baseball can continue.

articles.headline: Golf team finds strength in depth and consistency
articles.body: What excites senior Kale Patel most about golf is simple: the effortless strike of a flushed shot. The Sacramento Country Day golf team has 19 players with two seniors. The team isn’t built around one standout star; instead it’s a product of consistency, determination and putting the team first. The players say that this balance contributes to what separates them from other teams. “I think the main thing is that other teams have really good players, but they also have players that are not so great,” Patel said. “We’re all decent, and we also have strong players. We don’t really blow up. We’re very consistent.” On the golf team — where six players typically compete and the top five scores count — consistency can decide matches. Head coach Kristoffer Hall said that “the goal was to win leagues, and we didn’t lose a single tournament.” The team was undefeated in four league tournaments and was ranked fourth out of 16 teams in section championships, with Patel placing eighth out of 117 competitors. However, these placements were not the team’s only successes. According to Hall, you can only play six in a league tournament, and the team ended up having nine different golfers play in at least one league tournament. This team’s strength comes from the entire team, especially the bottom line, freshman Eddie Panfil said. “Normally, the fourth and fifth on the team would be really bad, shooting in the hundreds,” he said. Panfil said that team chemistry is just as important as talent. Instead of focusing only on individual rankings, teammates push each other to improve, offer advice and keep each other grounded during difficult rounds. “It’s very collaborative, very friendly,” Patel said. “We’re all trying to help each other. We’re not really focused entirely on our individual ranking and stuff, but we’re more focused as a team.” Patel said that one of the hardest things is learning to move on after a bad shot. Panfil expands on this. “Just taking it one shot at a time,” he said. “Not worrying too much about the bad shots, because good shots will come.” For freshman Mason Jung, motivation often comes from the team. Jung says that competition with teammates and friends helps him to improve, especially when his game feels inconsistent. “My friends help me get through it all,” Jung said. Jung has been playing since middle school, and his goals are to break 90 while improving his shot. Panfil is focusing on improving his putting game and believes that better work on the greens could have changed past tournament results. “My round at the small championships would have been way better if I just putted a little better,” he said. Patel has his sights set on postseason improvement. While each player has their own personal goals, their priorities remain with the team. Patel says that younger players earn opportunities through consistency and work ethic, while veterans like himself help make the transition easier. On April 28, Patel was announced as an A. Dale Lacky Student-Athlete Award winner. Every year, a male and female student athlete from each league within the Sac-Joaquin Section of the California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) is nominated for the A. Dale Lacky Memorial Scholarship — nominees are awarded $1,000 from the Section. Receivers of the scholarship showed “outstanding athletic performance, community service and academic success,” according to the CIF Sac-Joaquin website. “Yesterday [I was] playing golf, the day before [I was] playing golf. Not much time to study, playing golf all the time,” he said. In his scholarship essay, Patel referenced helping a struggling underclassman on the course. Jung added that upperclassmen play a major role in helping freshmen adjust. “The seniors help out the freshmen because they have more experience,” Jung said. Halls echoes this. “Our junior and senior leadership did a good job of bringing teammates into the fold,” Hall said. “Everyone contributed to the success of the team.”
